verifiedClaims.claim: If you hit an animal directly — such as striking a deer that runs into the road — this is typically covered under your comprehensive insurance policy (sometimes called "other than collision" coverage).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Triple-I, 'What is covered by a basic auto insurance policy?' ('collisions with deer are covered under comprehensive'); S.C. Department of Insurance, Automobile Insurance; NAIC Auto Insurance Database Report ('contact with a bird or animal')
verifiedClaims.note: Industry convention, not statute. Neither the Georgia Code nor the South Carolina Code assigns animal strikes to comprehensive coverage; the post correctly does not say a statute requires it (checked: no such statement anywhere in the body, takeaways or FAQs). The 'other than collision' label is the NAIC's own term.

verifiedClaims.claim: Comprehensive coverage pays to repair or replace your vehicle when damage results from events other than a collision with another vehicle. This includes animal strikes, falling objects, theft, vandalism, natural disasters, and fire.

verifiedClaims.note: III's list: contact with animals, natural disasters, fire, riots and vandalism, theft, fallen objects, broken windshield. Optional precision: 'other than a collision with another vehicle or object' (III's wording) since collision coverage also covers hitting a tree or pole.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia follows a modified comparative fault system under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. If you are injured in a swerve-to-avoid accident caused by loose livestock or a negligently controlled animal, you can recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault.
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1724/1756/1840 (verified this week): 'the plaintiff shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible'. Matches the writer-profile table.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia's statute of limitations for personal injury claims is 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). For property damage claims, the deadline is 4 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-31).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33; O.C.G.A. § 9-3-31 ('Actions for injuries to personalty shall be brought within four years')
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1840 (verified verbatim). § 9-3-31 is personal property, which a vehicle is.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under Georgia law, livestock owners have a duty to keep their animals properly fenced and confined (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3). If cattle, horses, or other livestock escape due to the owner's negligence and cause a car accident, the animal owner may be held liable for your injuries and vehicle damage.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3: 'No owner shall permit livestock to run at large on or to stray upon the public roads of this state or any property not belonging to the owner of the livestock, except by permission of the owner of such property.' Liability is negligence-based: a violation is not negligence per se (Porier v. Spivey, 97 Ga. App. 209 (1958); charging negligence per se is reversible error, Lovell v. Howard, 182 Ga. App. 891 (1987)); livestock running at large permits an inference that the owner was negligent, which disappears when the owner shows ordinary care in maintaining the stock (Green v. Heard Milling Co., 119 Ga. App. 116 (1969); Wilkins v. Beverly, 124 Ga. App. 842 (1971)); fences in good repair and closed gates defeated a driver's claim (West v. West, 299 Ga. App. 643 (2009)); the plaintiff must prove the defendant owned the animal (Taylor v. Thompkins, 242 Ga. App. 789 (2000)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3 and Justia annotations (2025 Code)
verifiedClaims.note: The section is cited correctly and the gist (owner may be liable if negligent) is right, but the statute does not say 'fenced' and the post omits the two things a reader needs: the owner is liable only for negligence, and a loose animal on the road lets a jury infer negligence unless the owner proves ordinary care. Suggested: 'Georgia's statewide livestock law makes it unlawful for an owner to let livestock run at large on a public road (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3). The owner is not automatically liable when an animal gets out: you must show negligence, but an animal loose on the road lets a jury infer the owner was negligent unless the owner proves ordinary care in fencing and confining it.'

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina also uses a modified comparative fault system. You can recover compensation if you are less than 51% at fault. The statute of limitations for personal injury claims is 3 years from the date of the accident (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991); S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1724/1756/1840 and the writer-profile table. Correctly uncited to any statute for the 51% bar; if a citation is added it must be Nelson, never § 15-38-15.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's livestock laws require animal owners to keep their animals properly enclosed. Under S.C. Code § 47-7-120, livestock owners can be held liable when their animals escape and cause accidents on public roadways.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Wrong section. S.C. Code § 47-7-120 ('Stock coming into State shall not be permitted to run at large') penalises anyone who brings horses, mules, hogs, cattle or sheep into South Carolina and lets them run at large 'in any marsh, forest lands or range' ($5 per head). The owner-liability rule is § 47-7-110: 'It shall be unlawful for the owner or manager of any domestic animal of any description wilfully or negligently to permit any such animal to run at large beyond the limits of his own land or the lands leased, occupied or controlled by him.' The South Carolina Supreme Court reads § 47-7-110 as a negligence standard, not an absolute duty: 'More than a showing of the presence of unattended animals on a highway is required. To recover under this statute, one must offer evidence from which a jury could infer at least negligence in permitting the animals to stray' (Reed v. Clark, 277 S.C. 310 (1982), citing McCullough v. Gatch, 251 S.C. 171 (1968)). § 47-7-130 makes the owner of stock found on another person's land liable for all damages sustained.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Title 47, Chapter 7, Article 3 (§§ 47-7-110, 47-7-120, 47-7-130); Reed v. Clark (S.C. 1982)
verifiedClaims.note: Replace § 47-7-120 with § 47-7-110 everywhere it appears (body, keyTakeaways, FAQ 2) and mirror the change on the Spanish twin. Suggested body wording: 'South Carolina makes it unlawful for an owner wilfully or negligently to let any domestic animal run at large beyond the owner's own land (S.C. Code § 47-7-110). The South Carolina Supreme Court has held that an animal loose on the highway is not enough by itself; you must offer evidence from which a jury could find the owner negligent in letting it stray.' 'Properly enclosed' is a fair gloss but 'require ... fenced' is not statutory language in either state.

verifiedClaims.claim: Counties may also have local fence ordinances that impose additional requirements.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 4-3-1 (Justia annotation: Hortman v. Guy, 242 Ga. App. 174 (2000) — § 4-3-1 'expressly preempts local laws on the subject by declaring the need for uniformity')
verifiedClaims.note: Sits in the South Carolina paragraph, but in Georgia the opposite is true (statewide law preempts local livestock ordinances), and no South Carolina county ordinance was verified. Unverifiable as written; remove.

verifiedClaims.claim: In both states, the minimum required auto insurance does not include comprehensive or collision coverage — only liability. Georgia requires minimum liability of 25/50/25 (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11), while South Carolina requires 25/50/25 (S.C. Code § 38-77-140).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Both minimums are 25/50/25 (Georgia: O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(1)(A) via § 40-9-37; South Carolina: § 38-77-140). But South Carolina's minimum policy is not 'only liability': every policy must also carry uninsured motorist coverage at the same limits and it cannot be rejected (§ 38-77-150(A)). Neither state's minimum includes comprehensive or collision.
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1724 (both statutes read verbatim this week). Suggested: 'In both states the legally required minimum is liability coverage (South Carolina also requires uninsured motorist coverage), and neither includes comprehensive or collision.' UM does not respond to an animal strike, so the conclusion stands. The limits and citations are correct.

verifiedClaims.claim: Call 911 — Report the accident, especially if there are injuries, significant vehicle damage, or the animal is blocking the roadway. A police report strengthens your insurance claim
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Reporting duties: Georgia — a driver must immediately notify local police (in a municipality) or the sheriff or state patrol when a crash causes injury, death or apparent property damage of $500 or more (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-273). South Carolina — immediate notice is required when a crash causes injury or death (§ 56-5-1260); if property damage is $1,000 or more and no officer investigated, a written report with proof of insurance must reach the SCDMV within 15 days (§ 56-5-1270).
verifiedClaims.note: The post states no threshold, so nothing is wrong; the thresholds are here in case the refresher wants one sentence. Note § 56-5-1260 has no dollar threshold at all (injury or death only); $1,000 belongs to § 56-5-1270's written-report rule. The deer-salvage rules are also verified if wanted: Georgia lets any person possess native wildlife accidentally killed by a motor vehicle, with a 48-hour notice requirement for bears and no right to protected species (O.C.G.A. § 27-3-28); SCDNR says a freshly killed deer may be kept 'as long as there is an incident report from the law enforcement officials that responded to the accident'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Do not approach the animal — Injured animals can be dangerous and unpredictable. Wait for animal control or wildlife officers
verifiedClaims.sourceName: State Farm Newsroom ('don't approach an injured or frightened animal'); SCDNR deer FAQ ('Badly injured deer should be euthanized by law enforcement officials that respond to the accident')

verifiedClaims.claim: If livestock was involved — Try to identify the animal's owner. Check for brands, ear tags, or nearby farms. This information is critical if you need to pursue a liability claim against the owner
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Taylor v. Thompkins, 242 Ga. App. 789 (2000) (summary judgment for defendant where plaintiff failed to show defendant owned the cow) — Justia annotation to § 4-3-3
verifiedClaims.note: Good advice with a case behind it: ownership must be proven.

verifiedClaims.claim: In both Georgia and South Carolina, a driver who swerves may be found partially or fully at fault if their reaction was unreasonable under the circumstances.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Both states recognise the sudden-emergency doctrine, which is the legal frame for this. Georgia: a driver 'confronted with a sudden emergency without sufficient time to determine with certainty the best course to pursue ... is not held to the same accuracy of judgment' (Rice v. Francis, Ga. App. 2025, quoting Smith v. Norfolk Southern); a charge on the doctrine was upheld where a driver swerved to avoid a deer and skidded into oncoming traffic (Stephens v. Hypes, 271 Ga. App. 863 (2005)); the doctrine requires a choice of conduct and does not protect a driver whose own negligence created the emergency. South Carolina: a driver 'confronted with a sudden emergency brought about by the negligence of another and not by his own negligence ... is not guilty of negligence if he makes such a choice as a person of ordinary prudence placed in such a position might make' (McVey v. Whittington, 248 S.C. 447 (1966)); it does not apply when the party's own negligence (e.g. speed) created the emergency (Clark v. Cantrell, 339 S.C. 369 (2000)); since comparative negligence it is a factor in the fault allocation rather than a complete bar (Haley v. Brown, 370 S.C. 63 (Ct. App. 2006)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Stephens v. Hypes (Ga. Ct. App. 2005); Rice v. Francis (Ga. Ct. App. 2025); McVey v. Whittington (S.C. 1966); Clark v. Cantrell (S.C. 2000); Haley v. Brown (S.C. Ct. App. 2006)
verifiedClaims.note: The post's list of factors (speed, time to stop, conditions, proportionality, adjacent lanes) tracks the doctrine's 'reasonably prudent person under the same circumstances' test. Optional one-sentence addition naming the doctrine: 'Both states apply the sudden-emergency doctrine: a driver who reacts reasonably to a deer that appears without warning is not negligent for failing to make the wisest choice, but the doctrine does not protect a driver whose own speed or inattention created the emergency.' Stephens v. Hypes is a deer-swerve case on point for Georgia.

verifiedClaims.claim: Fencing obligations — Both states generally require livestock owners to keep animals fenced. A broken or poorly maintained fence can establish negligence
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Both states make it unlawful for an owner to permit livestock to run at large (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3; S.C. Code § 47-7-110). Fence condition is the usual evidence: fencing in good repair and closed gates defeated the driver's claim in West v. West, 299 Ga. App. 643 (2009); evidence of the owner's care in maintaining the pasture fence goes to the jury (Green v. Heard Milling Co.).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3 (Justia annotations); S.C. Code § 47-7-110
verifiedClaims.note: Substance is right; wording should track the statutes ('let livestock run at large') rather than a fencing mandate neither code contains. Suggested: 'Both states make it unlawful for an owner to let livestock run at large (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3; S.C. Code § 47-7-110). A broken or poorly maintained fence is the usual evidence of negligence; a fence in good repair with closed gates has defeated claims.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Premises liability principles may also apply if the animal escaped from adjacent property due to the landowner's negligence.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: In Georgia the duty under Chapter 4-3 runs to the animal's 'owner' as defined in § 4-3-2(2); a pasture owner who let her son keep his horse there was not an 'owner' and was 'under no obligation to prevent the horse from escaping' (Supchak v. Pruitt, 232 Ga. App. 680).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3 Justia annotation (Supchak v. Pruitt)
verifiedClaims.note: No authority found in either state for landowner (non-owner) liability on a premises theory for an escaped animal, and Georgia authority cuts the other way. Remove the sentence, or the internal link with it; keep the homeowner's/farm-liability-policy sentence, which is about the owner's insurance, not the landowner.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Directly striking an animal is typically covered under comprehensive insurance, not collision. You will pay your comprehensive deductible, and this type of claim generally does not increase your insurance premiums.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Yes, if you carry comprehensive coverage. Directly striking an animal is typically a comprehensive claim, not collision. You will pay your comprehensive deductible; insurers usually treat the claim as not-at-fault, so it is less likely than an at-fault collision claim to raise your premium, though it can still affect claims-free discounts.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: State Farm, 'Will my insurance increase after a claim?'; Triple-I

verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Accurate and appropriately hedged.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Under Georgia law (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3) and South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 47-7-120), livestock owners have a duty to keep their animals properly fenced. If they fail to do so and their animal causes a car accident, they can be held liable for injuries and damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Yes, if the owner was negligent. Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 47-7-110) both make it unlawful for an owner to let livestock run at large. Neither state makes the owner automatically liable when an animal gets out: you must show the owner failed to use ordinary care in fencing and confining it, though in Georgia an animal loose on the road lets a jury infer negligence unless the owner proves that care.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3 and annotations; S.C. Code § 47-7-110; Reed v. Clark (S.C. 1982)
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data, so the wrong section number is published twice. Two corrections: § 47-7-120 to § 47-7-110, and 'duty to keep fenced' to the negligence standard both states apply.

verifiedClaims.claim: No. If you carry only the minimum liability insurance required by Georgia or South Carolina law, you have no coverage for damage to your own vehicle from an animal strike. Only comprehensive coverage protects against animal collision damage.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Triple-I, 'What is covered by a basic auto insurance policy?'; S.C. Department of Insurance
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Correct; uninsured motorist coverage (mandatory in South Carolina) does not respond because no other motorist is involved.

verifiedClaims.claim: Pull over safely, call 911, do not approach the animal, photograph the damage and scene, check for injuries, and file a comprehensive insurance claim promptly. A police report strengthens your claim.

verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Optional: 'Georgia requires a report when damage appears to be $500 or more; South Carolina requires one for any injury.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Deer-vehicle collisions peak during October through December — the deer mating season (rut). During this period, deer are more active and more likely to cross roadways, especially at dawn and dusk.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: State Farm (November, October, December are the top months nationally); SCDNR ('typically from October to November ... about 45% of deer-vehicle collisions occur during this time ... Most vehicle collisions occur near dawn and dusk')
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Optional precision for South Carolina: SCDNR puts the peak rut at the last two weeks of October through the first two weeks of November, with 83% of does bred between Oct. 6 and Nov. 16 (2024 Deer Harvest Report).

recommendedEdits: Body, intro: replace the dead III link (404) and the unsourced 'thousands of injuries' with 'State Farm estimates more than 1.6 million animal-collision insurance claims nationwide between July 2025 and June 2026, and the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety counted 210 deaths in animal-collision crashes in 2024'; link to https://www.iii.org/fact-statistic/facts-statistics-deer-vehicle-collisions or the State Farm release.

Body, 'How Animal-Related Car Accidents Happen': replace 'Georgia consistently ranks among the top 15 states ...' with State Farm's 2025-26 odds: Georgia 1 in 115 (22nd), South Carolina 1 in 103 (18th), national 1 in 145.
Body: drop the US-17 / I-26 sentence; replace with 'The S.C. Department of Public Safety recorded 6,628 reported deer-vehicle collisions statewide in 2024' (SCDNR 2024 Deer Harvest Report, Table 11).
Body, feral hog bullet: remove 'increasing' ('A hazard in rural areas of both states').

Body and FAQ 0 and comparison table: hedge the rate claim — 'usually treated as not-at-fault and less likely than an at-fault collision claim to raise your premium, though it can still affect claims-free discounts'; table cells 'Usually no rate increase' become 'Often not chargeable; varies by insurer'.

Body, Georgia livestock paragraph: keep § 4-3-3 but say what it does — unlawful to let livestock run at large on public roads; liability requires negligence (not negligence per se); a loose animal lets a jury infer negligence unless the owner proves ordinary care.

Body, South Carolina livestock paragraph, keyTakeaways and FAQ 2: change S.C. Code § 47-7-120 to § 47-7-110 (three surfaces, one of them FAQPage structured data) and describe it as a wilful-or-negligent standard; the Supreme Court requires evidence of negligence beyond the animal's presence on the highway (Reed v. Clark).
Body: delete 'Counties may also have local fence ordinances that impose additional requirements.'
Body, insurance-minimums paragraph: change 'only liability' to 'liability coverage (South Carolina also requires uninsured motorist coverage)'; limits and citations stay.

Body, 'Livestock on the Road' fencing bullet: reword to 'Both states make it unlawful for an owner to let livestock run at large (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3; S.C. Code § 47-7-110)'; fence condition is the evidence of negligence.
Body: delete the premises-liability sentence (Georgia: a landowner who is not the animal's owner has no duty under § 4-3-3, Supchak v. Pruitt); the homeowner's/farm-policy sentence stays.
Excerpt: 'different policies' to 'different coverages' (it publishes as the Article description).

Optional, swerving section: one sentence naming the sudden-emergency doctrine in both states, with Stephens v. Hypes (Ga. App. 2005, a deer-swerve case) and Clark v. Cantrell (S.C. 2000) as the authorities.

Optional, 'What to Do' step 2: reporting thresholds — Georgia $500 apparent property damage or any injury (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-273); South Carolina any injury (§ 56-5-1260), plus a written SCDMV report within 15 days if damage is $1,000 or more and no officer investigated (§ 56-5-1270).

Optional, 'What to Do': deer salvage — Georgia allows possession of native wildlife accidentally killed by a vehicle (O.C.G.A. § 27-3-28); South Carolina allows keeping a freshly killed deer with the responding officer's incident report (SCDNR).
Mirror every changed figure and the § 47-7-110 correction on the Spanish twin; record Graeham C. Gillin as reviewer (two-state post that states South Carolina law).

statuteCitations.name: Legislative intent — uniform statewide livestock law embracing all public roads (Ga. L. 1953, 1955); preempts local livestock ordinances (Hortman v. Guy); the chapter abolished Georgia's open range

Permitting livestock to run at large or stray — no owner shall permit livestock to run at large on or stray upon the public roads; negligence standard, not negligence per se; loose livestock permits an inference of negligence rebuttable by proof of ordinary care
Reduction and apportionment of award or bar of recovery according to percentage of fault (50% bar, subsection (g))
Injuries to the person — two years
Uninsured motorist coverage under motor vehicle liability policies (minimum limits 25/50/25 in (a)(1)(A))
Requirements for liability insurance policies (limits not less than § 33-7-11(a)(1)(A))
Duty to report accident resulting in injury, death, or property damage — immediate notice when apparent property damage is $500 or more
Person may take possession of native wildlife accidentally killed by a motor vehicle (48-hour notice for bears; protected species excluded)

Permitting domestic animals to run at large unlawful — owner or manager may not wilfully or negligently permit any domestic animal to run at large beyond his own land (the owner-liability statute; Reed v. Clark)

Stock coming into State shall not be permitted to run at large — $5-per-head penalty for stock brought into South Carolina and left at large in marsh, forest or range (NOT a general owner-liability statute; the post miscites it)
Liability of owners of trespassing stock — owner liable for all damages when animals are found on another's land
Minimum liability limits — $25,000 per person, $50,000 per accident, $25,000 property damage
Uninsured motorist coverage mandatory in every policy at the § 38-77-140 limits; cannot be rejected
Three years — injury to the person (5); wrongful death from date of death (6)
Immediate report of accidents resulting in personal injury or death (no property-damage threshold)
Written report to SCDMV within 15 days when injury, death or total property damage of $1,000 or more and no law enforcement investigation

McVey v. Whittington, 248 S.C. 447 (1966) — South Carolina sudden-emergency rule
Clark v. Cantrell, 339 S.C. 369 (2000) — sudden-emergency doctrine unavailable where the driver's own negligence created the emergency
Haley v. Brown, 370 S.C. 63 (Ct. App. 2006) — sudden emergency is a factor in the comparative-fault analysis
